Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Omar, a 27-year-old physical therapist, sat stiffly in the chair, his hands clasped so tightly his knuckles were white. The event had happened six months ago, but speaking of it felt like trying to describe a scene from a movie he’d been forced to watch, one where he was both the audience and the unwilling star. He often found himself thinking of it that way, as if it had happened to someone else, a character whose life briefly and horrifically intersected with his own. It started with a referral for his own persistent shoulder pain. He’d booked a deep tissue massage with a practitioner who came highly recommended. The room had been dimly lit, smelling strongly of an oud-based cologne that clung to the air. At first, the session was routine, but then the man’s touch changed. When Omar tried to pull away, he was held down, the pressure on his injured shoulder becoming a sharp, searing pain that silenced his protest. The scent of the cologne was suffocating, and the pain became the anchor to a reality he couldn't escape.

In the weeks that followed, Omar’s world began to shrink. At his clinic, the familiar environment became a minefield. The sudden movement of a patient reaching for a water bottle behind him would cause him to jolt, his muscles tensing for a blow that never came. A well-meaning colleague once clapped him on the shoulder in greeting, and Omar flinched so violently he nearly knocked over a cart of equipment. He was certain that any unexpected touch was a threat, a prelude to being overpowered again. He began constantly monitoring his own body, pressing into the muscles of his shoulder and back, checking for soreness or tension, as if he could locate the lingering physical evidence of the violation. He felt ashamed of what had happened to his body, a feeling that intensified whenever he caught his reflection. He couldn't rely on himself, he reasoned; his own body had frozen, had failed to protect him, and now it was a constant, humiliating reminder of that failure.

The assault followed him home, seeping into the most intimate parts of his life. His wife, Layla, tried to be patient, but Omar would freeze at her touch. Any attempt at intimacy would send a jolt of panic through him, and he would pull away, leaving a chasm of hurt silence between them. The triggers were everywhere. A man walked past him in a department store wearing a similar heavy cologne, and Omar had to rush to the bathroom, gagging. Any flare-up of his old shoulder injury brought not just physical discomfort but a vivid, sensory replay of being pinned down. To manage this, he threw himself into his work, taking on extra shifts and staying late, doing anything to exhaust his mind and body so he wouldn't have to think about the event. But the exhaustion only led to a profound numbness. He watched Layla’s worry turn to frustration, saw the love in her eyes dim, and felt nothing. It was this emotional void that frightened him most; he had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the capacity for joy, love, and connection had been permanently scoured out of him.

It was Layla who finally broke the silence. One evening, after another failed attempt to hold his hand, she sat across from him and told him, her voice trembling, that she felt she was married to a ghost. She missed her husband, the man who laughed and felt things, and she was afraid he was gone for good. Her words cut through the fog of his avoidance. The thought of losing her, of his career unraveling because of his startle response, was more terrifying than confronting the memory itself. He made the appointment the next day, driven by a desperate, flickering hope. He was afraid he was irrevocably broken, but a small part of him wondered if it was possible to feel like himself again, to inhabit his own body without shame, and to once again feel the warmth of his wife’s hand without flinching away.
